articles.text: An earthquake was felt throughout Piedmont and the rest of the East Bay early Monday morning. Residents woke up in the night to feel rumbling at 2:56 a.m. on Monday, September 22. The 4.3 magnitude quake was centered in Berkeley a few blocks south of the UC Berkeley Campus. Piedmont Firefighters felt the quake, assessing the Fire Station for damage and found no problems. In spite of the sharp and loud jolt and the brief rumbling sound, the earthquake did not result in any calls for service. Piedmont Public Works received no calls regarding the earthquake as well. “This earthquake is a good reminder to review your household emergency communication plan and home disaster supply kit and make sure you know what to do when you feel shaking – drop, cover, and hold on,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The earthquake’s origin point was close to the Hayward Fault, which experts estimate has a one in three chance of experiencing a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in the next 30 years, according to an earthquake outlook published in 2019. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has an aftershock predictor that indicates about an 18% chance of another earthquake greater than magnitude 3.0 in the surrounding region in the next week. Chances of a more significant event drop off quickly, though there is about a 2% probability of an aftershock greater than magnitude 4.0 in that same time. articles.text: On September 19th students at Piedmont Middle School held the Medieval Faire. New 7th graders looked forward to it as a fun way to tie in their newfound knowledge of the Middle Ages after learning about it the few weeks prior. This event included a medieval banquet, where core classes performed skits and dances. Ms. Brenneman’s AM core class did a Maypole dance, a traditional medieval performance. They took ribbons and wrapped them around a pole, which signifies fertility, spring, and community. Mr. Scherman’s AM class carried out a skit which taught everyone about table manners. Ms. Kelly’s class even did a dance with sticks, hitting them together and doing moves that mimic sword fighting. “The performances were very fun and coordinated, everyone did so well!” said 7th grader Nina Stock. Additionally, there were also fun booths that other core classes ran. Overall, the function was full of fun and games, and needless to say, 7th graders enjoyed the hour and a half long entertainment. articles.text: In the time it takes to enjoy a cup of coffee, your family can become more confident and prepared for a wildfire. As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. Follow i ng step -by-step instructions and discussion prompts provided in a short video, families, housemates, and neighbors can transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. In less than an hour, this exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of evacuation • A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps • A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process • Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfireDrill. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. Building a more prepared community The at-home evacuation exercise is one part the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. This summer, the Department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide yearround public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. Last year the Department also led development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the City could take to reduce the impacts of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
articles.title: Fire Dept. asks residents to complete at-home wildfire evacuation exercise

Meanwhile, those who do not want to share our parks with our dog friends have all the lawns at Piedmont Park. Bear Park, the lawns at both the top and bottom of Dracena Quarry, and all the sports fields. articles.text: The following is an abridged version of the Piedmont Pulse, a bi-weekly update, published by the Superintendent of Piedmont Unified School District, Jennifer Hawn. The unabridged version is available at Smore.com/n/gt0zk September 22 Dear PUSD Families & Staff: Last week I had a chance to attend the 6th grade new family night, the 7th grade new family night, and the City’s new families night. Building community is at the heart of Piedmont, and I firmly believe that when we bring our parents together, our kids also build stronger relationships with each other. Speaking of our kids, I hosted a lunch for our high school students to hear their thoughts on how the cell phone policy is going at PHS/MHS. Our kids are so wise and had many effective arguments for the use of phones at the high school level. Some students (well...only a few) also commented that the new policy is something they can live with, but expressed concern about a more restrictive policy next year. Hearing the experiences of parents and our students reminds me of the importance of listening to all members of our school community: students, staff, and parents, in our efforts to offer the finest education possible. I encourage our families to continue to engage in the many community opportunities below to share perspective on our school programs. Your voice matters. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent High School Courses Two weeks ago, I wrote [smore. com/n/nas4p6] about the challenges of the high school schedule of courses, including our efforts to offer courses according to student interest and need. To further improve our efforts, we held a Board workshop on September 12th to explore options that could improve course opportunities for students, including transitioning to graduation requirements that reflect the UC A-G course admission requirements. At this workshop, we defined courses according to the California State high school graduation requirements, the UC A-G course requirements, and reviewed our PUSD high school graduation requirements [docs.google. com/spreadsheets/d/16ut-_GwBwAu7iKswzRXchvId2CBDKcTwhwDjCkXiDq0/edit?usp=sharing]. All three sets of requirements are different, and we discussed PUSD courses that we may want to change from a requirement to an elective option. Semester courses under consideration include the following: • Computer Studies • Ethnic Studies • Health To be clear, the rationale for moving these courses from a requirement to an elective option is to allow students more flexibility to pursue courses that reflect their interests and needs. At the workshop, we also reviewed enrollment in elective courses, with consideration of criteria to use when we determine we should not offer a course. We currently have under-enrolled elective courses that prompted a discussion of the cost to offer a course, which comes to a minimum of 24 students. That is, when we offer courses under 24 students, the revenue we receive for each student does not cover the cost of the course. We already cover the cost of many courses that have under 24 students for some core and other required courses, and so it is not financially sustainable to offer elective courses that are under-enrolled. In order to ensure a balance between providing robust course offerings and financial sustainability, we are developing a rubric to use for elective courses. This rubric will take into account various criteria, including course requests, lab courses, access for alternative learners, new courses, cost, and actual enrollment in the current year and over time. A review of this year’s course options revealed challenges for students to access the courses they requested. Enrollment for some elective courses is unsustainably low; however, we have heard from teachers that enrollment does not reflect student interest. Conversely, we have courses that have high demand, sometimes over-enrolled and unavailable, leaving students forced to choose courses they did not request, including “Unscheduled” free periods and/ or TA periods instead of electives students want. At the September 24th Board meeting, we will follow up on information the Board requested. No decisions will be made at this meeting; however, we will provide additional information from the 9/12 Board workshop on how we can move forward with improving our process for offering high school course options that meet the interests and needs of our students.

articles.text: Screens are everywhere – phones, tablets, TVs, laptops, Children today are surrounded by them from a very young age. While technology brings many benefits, from virtual storybooks to video calls with grandparents, parents often wonder: How much screen time is too much? And what does it mean for my child’s speech and language development? What the research tells us Studies have shown that children under the age of two learn best through real-life, face-toface interactions. Talking, playing, and reading with caregivers provide the foundation for language development. When screen time replaces these interactions, children may miss out on valuable opportunities to practice back-and-forth communication. For preschool and school-age children, the effects are more nuanced. Educational programs and interactive apps can support learning, but passive viewing— like watching videos alone— doesn’t promote the same level of language growth as conversation-rich activities. In fact, children who spend more time in front of screens may have smaller vocabularies and weaker social communication skills. Quality matters more than quantity It’s not just about how much time children spend on screens— it’s about how they use them. A video chat with a grandparent, where your child responds and asks questions, is very different from passively watching cartoons. “Co-viewing” (watching together and talking about what you see) makes a big difference. For example, if your child is watching a show about animals, pause and ask, “What sound does that lion make?” or “Which animal do you like best?” This turns screen time into an interactive language-building experience. Guidelines for families The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) offers helpful recommendations: • Under 18 months: Avoid screen time, except for video chatting. • 18–24 months: If you introduce screens, choose high-quality programming and watch together. • Ages 2–5: Limit screen time to about one hour per day of quality content, with co-viewing encouraged. • Ages 6 and up: Place consistent limits on time and content, ensuring screen use doesn’t replace sleep, physical activity, or family interaction. Practical tips for parents • Prioritize Face-to-Face: Even short bursts of play and conversation during daily routines (mealtime, bath time, car rides) support language more than passive screen use.

articles.text: With Homecoming approaching this Saturday, Piedmont High School kicked off Spirit Week on Monday. Spirit Week is a long-standing PHS tradition designed to rally students in the lead-up to Homecoming, culminating in Friday’s Purple Out and the highly anticipated Homecoming football game Friday evening. The week not only celebrates school pride but also encourages friendly competition and creativity among students across grade levels. The daily themes are: PJ Day, Mountain vs. Beach, Upperclassmen as Seniors vs. Underclassmen as Babies, Wild West vs. West Coast, and a Friday Purple Out. Students are encouraged to dress according to each theme. ASB decorated the school’s interiors over the weekend to spark excitement and build school spirit. Often, however, ASB struggles to fully engage the entire student body. Even though they visit classrooms the week before Spirit Week and post engaging videos to remind students of the themes and encourage participation, turnout and enthusiasm during the week often fall short of expectations. Many students seem less motivated to dress up or join in the rally activities compared to past years, making it a challenge for ASB to generate the same level of school spirit from previous Spirit Weeks. “I feel like Spirit Week is really fun, but sometimes the themes repeat a lot because ASB has limited options, so people don’t always get excited,” said PHS senior Amelia Carter. “I’ve also noticed that if seniors don’t participate, underclassmen follow suit. Last year, the current sophomore class didn’t participate much, which is a little frustrating. They might think they’re too cool for it, even though dressing up can be really fun.” Monday’s theme is “PJ Day” giving everyone a comfortable option to start the week. “I think seniors need to lead the charge so more students will join in and I’m actually really excited to dress up for every theme. On the bright side, ASB’s publicity has improved, so hopefully that helps boost participation,” added Carter. Spirit Week will culminate with the entire city piling on the community spirit as the Piedmont Highlander football teams hosts Arroyo High at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m. on Friday. Photo by Evolette Mak Seniors Rachel Young (left), Meher Baccher, Chloe Koh, Stephanie Lee, Elisha Bell, Elena O’Connell, and Sacha Andrews show off their Pajamas for Piedmont High School’s Spirit Week.

The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. Homecoming starts with Spirit Week By Evolette Mak With Homecoming approaching this Saturday, Piedmont High School kicked off Spirit Week on Monday. Spirit Week is a long-standing PHS tradition designed to rally students in the lead-up to Homecoming, culminating in Friday’s Purple Out and the highly anticipated Homecoming football game Friday evening. The week not only celebrates school pride but also encourages friendly competition and creativity among students across grade levels. The daily themes are: PJ Day, Mountain vs. Beach, Upperclassmen as Seniors vs. Underclassmen as Babies, Wild West vs. West Coast, and a Friday Purple Out. Students are encouraged to dress according to each theme. ASB decorated the school’s interiors over the weekend to spark excitement and build school spirit. Often, however, ASB struggles to fully engage the entire student body. Even though they visit classrooms the week before Spirit Week and post engaging videos to remind students of the themes and encourage participation, turnout and enthusiasm during the week often fall short of expectations. Many students seem less motivated to dress up or join in the rally activities compared to past years, making it a challenge for ASB to generate the same level of school spirit from previous Spirit Weeks. “I feel like Spirit Week is really fun, but sometimes the themes repeat a lot because ASB has limited options, so people don’t always get excited,” said PHS senior Amelia Carter. “I’ve also noticed that if seniors don’t participate, underclassmen follow suit. Last year, the current sophomore class didn’t participate much, which is a little frustrating. They might think they’re too cool for it, even though dressing up can be really fun.” Monday’s theme is “PJ Day” giving everyone a comfortable option to start the week. “I think seniors need to lead the charge so more students will join in and I’m actually really excited to dress up for every theme. On the bright side, ASB’s publicity has improved, so hopefully that helps boost participation,” added Carter. Spirit Week will culminate with the entire city piling on the community spirit as the Piedmont Highlander football teams hosts Arroyo High at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m. on Friday. articles.text: This year’s Medieval Faire had a variety of costumes worn by nobles and knights, peasants and merchants. This year’s King, Kai Chiles, and Queen, Sophie Messina, wore extravagant costumes, with shining crowns and luxurious robes, making their presence very noticeable in the dining hall. Lords and Ladies who sat at the front table had some noticeable costumes themselves. It seems that some had a lot of effort and planning in them. The nobles had flashy robes, and some, tiaras, and other luxurious accessories. One Lord, Oliver Dewar, took noblewear to the next level, wearing shades of purple, black, and gold with a black dotted lustrous robe. A very common and simple type of costume was that of a merchant. A baggy linen shirt with some kind of leather vest, and a nice leather belt with pants was a popular costume for the average citizen (and this author). Although people were very creative about it! Some wore green pants, some wore dark green pants, some wore brown, some wore light brown, and even red! The dining hall was full of merchants! Though there were a lot of merchants and peasants, there were also bakers. Miles Croan Smolko and Zain Shah were bakers and called themselves Big Little Bakery! A white apron, stained with chocolate or baking flour, spread across the face of this dessert disher costume. Teachers had some costumes to be reckoned with as well. Many had impressive dresses or gowns with green or other medieval colors. The most intriguing costume I saw was Mr. Scherman, who used a brown robe with a rope for a belt and was a friar! Incredibly creative costume! Although there were some basic costumes, there were many amazing ones that had a lot of thought put into them. Overall, for this Medieval Faire, the costumes were a win. Like I said, from nobles and knights to peasants and merchants, these medieval costumes are the best part of the faire. Staff Photos Scherman’s Morning Manor teaches the entire medieval gala about good table manners. Wesley Kolstad (left), Gabriel Garrigues, Curtis Broome (with mic), Ezra Schwartz (with book) and Emi Ito and Olive Abelson Lindsey wait for a chance to douse their favorite teachers. The most popular activity was the olliebollen-on-a-string contest, which entails competitors racing to eat an olliebollen attached to a piece of thread. An olliebollen is a fourteenth-century name for a doughnut. After the contenders had faced their doughnuts, there was no trace of the sugary snack left, just a sprinkling of crumbs. Cornhole, fortune telling, and the marriage booth were also fun and popular additions to the activities of the faire.

articles.text: Alive with energy and excitement, the Medieval Festival was filled with a variety of games meant to indulge students in the fun of medieval life. Par ticipants wanting to unlock their inner jester participated in stilt walking. In medieval times, stilts were used for maneuvering through marshes and flooded land, but here at Piedmont Middle School, they were used for fun. Students enticed by more dangerous activities gravitated to sword fighting. The rules are simple: two opponents are handed weaponry, pool noodles, and fight for a serving of seafood (Swedish fish). Whoever hits their rival twice with their pool noodle sword under the shoulders wins and is rewarded. The festival also included the traditional medieval practice of public humiliation and physical punishment. Volunteering teachers were locked in wooden pillories and exposed to public ridicule, scorn, and wet sponges in a game of soak-a-bloke. During the banquet, lords and ladies took their seats above the rest at their “C” shaped table facing the crowd, while the royalty was welcomed into the hall with another dance. They sat upon their thrones and welcomed everyone in the room. Nobles took the responsibility of giving a speech thanking the king and queen and calling the manor’s citizens to stand and cheer. After the delightful entertainment provided by the citizens of multiple manors and the informative etiquette lesson, the king and queen called for the beginning of the feast. Among the citizens feasting, their roles were quite simple, like peasants. Obviously, there were many a pope, priest, and plague doctor playing out their roles perfectly. Aside from the medieval roles people took on, we were also able to volunteer to work at faire booths. While working these jobs, students really got into character like a fortune teller who told my fortune, Winne Schickedanz, who played her role perfectly. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team took third place at the Vintage Valley Tournament in Napa over the weekend. Piedmont High took third place at the 2025 Vintage Valley Water Polo Tournament at Vintage High School in Napa last weekend, September 19-20. Piedmont opened the tournament with an 11-9 win over Roseville, lost 17-7 to Liberty, and beat Carmel narrowly 14-13 to close. It was a strong game for Henry Stein against Carmel with six goals in their win to claim third place. Elles Kreickhaus was important in a 11-9 win over Roseville, leading the team with four goals. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 6-5 overall. They now look ahead to the start of their league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont faced league rival Berkeley on Tuesday and will visit Castro Valley on Thursday, September 25. 14-13 over Carmel Piedmont led 5-2 after the first quarter and held an 8-5 lead by halftime. Carmel narrowed the deficit to 11-9 in the third quarter and outscored the Highlanders 4-3 in the fourth quarter but PHS scored the game-winner with 55 seconds left. In the first quarter, Carmel scored quickly after just 22 seconds, but the Highlanders scored four straight goals with three straight by Henry Stein to claim an early hat trick, and one by Rylan Patty to give PHS a 5-1 lead with 37 seconds left. Carmel got one back with 17 seconds remaining. Piedmont drew a man-advantage after 33 seconds in the second quarter, leading to another goal by Stein. After a pair of Padre goals, Elles Kreickhaus scored at the 1:38 mark. Carmel scored with 31 seconds left, but 12 answered on the ensuing possession with six seconds on the clock. Carmel scored to open the third with a goal after 30 seconds, but the Padres committed a foul, leading to Stein scoring his fifth. Carmel scored the next two goals to cut Piedmont’s lead to 9-8 with 2:56 remaining, but PHS responded with two straight goals by Kreickhaus and Ben Kappas. The Padres scored once more with 29 seconds remaining, making it 11-9. In the fourth, Carmel scored quickly to cut the lead to one. But with 4:20 left, Piedmont scored with a man-advantage for a 12-10 lead. But the Padres knotted things up at 12-12 with 3:09 remaining. Colin Amen scored with 1:43 left, but Carmel tied it just 13 seconds later. With 55 seconds left in the game, Patty launched in the eventual game-winner, and Piedmont held on defensively. Final stats: Stein had six goals, Patty scored three, Kreickhaus had two, and Kappas had one. 17-7 loss to Liberty Piedmont kept things close in the first quarter, going into the second down 4-3. However, Liberty, a Div. I school, extended its advantage to 9-5 in the second Photos by Lynne Wright Henry Stein logged six goals against Carmel to help PHS win a razorthin victory, 14-13.

A modern-day Renaissance man, he plays the violin, speaks fluent Farsi and French, holds a degree in Biomedical Engineering from the University of Minnesota, and is an award-winning product manager at a leading software company. In high school, Coach P was a recruited track athlete and also played football, experiences that gave him firsthand insight into the discipline, hard work, and sacrifice required of student athletes as they balance academics, athletics, and personal growth. He brings that perspective to every practice and uses it to guide and mentor the athletes he coaches. Coach P leads with a “players first” philosophy and relentless energy. He inspires athletes to push past their limits and build their conditioning both in-season and out. Under his leadership, the track program has reached unprecedented heights. The boys’ team captured the first league titles in school history, and more than twenty athletes have earned spots on college rosters. Off the field, he is a proud Minnesotan, a lifelong Vikings fan, a husband, and a new parent. Known as one of the best time managers around, Coach P balances his family life, a demanding career, and his coaching responsibilities. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will present the first major retrospective of painter Suzanne Jackson, entitled Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love, opening September 27 and running through March 1, 2026. Organized in collaboration with the artist, the exhibition spans six decades of Jackson’s multifaceted career. Featuring more than 80 works, including paintings, drawings, and a new large-scale commission, the show explores Jackson’s novel approach to color, light, and structure, as well as her deep connection to nature, poetry, and performance. Jackson is known for her ethereal early canvases and her recent three-dimensional “floating” acrylic paintings that challenge traditional notions of painting. The exhibition also examines her interdisciplinary background as a dancer, poet, and theater designer, highlighting how these influences and her ties to radical artist communities shaped her art. “Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love promises to be a groundbreaking exhibition,” said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director. “Jackson continues to innovate by extending paint into three dimensions and embedding it with found materials to reflect on personal and cultural histories.” “Suzanne Jackson’s life has been driven by an insistent search for creative freedom and a bohemian spirit that is indebted to the San Francisco ethos in which she was raised,” added Jenny Gheith, curator of the exhibition and SFMOMA’s Interim Head of Painting and Sculpture. “What Is Love captures the curiosity, wonder and resilience of Jackson’s life’s work.” Jackson will participate in an artist talk at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art on Thursday, September 25 at 5 p.m. with scholar Kellie Jones, chair of the African American and African Diaspora Studies Department at Columbia University. In her conversation with Jones, Jackson will reflect on her creative process, her experience across artistic disciplines and her relationship to the Bay Area. On Friday, September 26 SFMOMA will invite several speakers to discuss different aspects of the artist’s work for the Suzanne Jackson and Friends program. The event begins at 6 p.m. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. Artist Suzanne Jackson

articles.text: The Exploratorium in San Francisco hosts its 26th annual Engineering Day, with events conducted in Spanish and English, this Saturday, September 27. Engineering Day offers hands-on activities and cultural experiences aimed to spark children’s curiosity in science and technology. This year’s programming focuses on electrical, structural, mechanical, aerospace, and biological interactive activities, including a build-your-own catapult workshop, a presentation on bridge structural integrity, and a hands-on water quality test alongside experts from Engineers Without Borders. articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present two performances of Dead Man Walking at the War Memorial Opera House from September 26 and 28, marking the 25th anniversary of the opera’s world premiere. Commissioned by San Francisco Opera and first performed in 2000, Dead Man Walking is composed by Jake Heggie with a libretto by Terrence McNally. The opera is based on the 1993 memoir by Sister Helen Prejean, which recounts her experiences with a death-row inmate. Since its premiere, the work has been staged over 80 times globally and is now considered the most performed contemporary opera in the repertoire. “This production of Dead Man Walking represents one of the most astonishing, full-circle moments of my career,” Heggie said in a press release. “It’s hard to believe it was 25 years ago when the opera premiered here to phenomenal acclaim. No one could have predicted the journey it would make, with more than 80 international productions to date.” The 25th-anniversary presentation features mezzo-soprano Jamie Barton as Sister Helen Prejean and bass-baritone Ryan McKinny as Joseph De Rocher, the condemned inmate. Susan Graham, who originated the role of Sister Helen in 2000, returns to the opera as Mrs. Patrick De Rocher. Patrick Summers, who conducted the premiere, returns to lead the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and Chorus. The production is directed by Leonard Foglia, with set designs by Michael McGarty and costume design by Jess Goldstein. The staging, originally developed by a consortium of American opera companies, is owned by Lyric Opera of Chicago and is being presented at the War Memorial Opera House for the first time this year. Additional cast members include Brittany Renee as Sister Rose, Raymond Aceto as George Benton, Rod Gilfry and Caroline Corrales as Owen and Kitty Hart, and Nikola Printz and Samuel White as Jade and Howard Boucher. Dead Man Walking is performed in English with English supertitles. Performance dates are September 26 (7:30 p.m.) and 28 (2 p.m.). Call the San Francisco box office at (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera.com to purchase tickets. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Shotgun Players Christopher Chen’s The Motion premiered on the Ashby Stage September 13. Shotgun Players presents the world premiere of Christopher Chen’s The Motion, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through October 12. Obie Award–winner Christopher Chen blurs the line between performance and participation in his newest play The Motion, where a heated debate slips down a kaleidoscopic ‘rabbit hole’ engaging audience members as voyeurs and accomplices. Theater guests are given voting cards and are invited to take part in the experience as it happens on stage. The Motion is a unique play that entwines clever comedy, sharp dialogue, and science fiction to create a fractal pattern of moral dilemmas. “The Motion, which riffs on the debate format before spinning into different worlds, is one of the most ambitious plays I’ve written,” said Chen. “There’s a particular thrill when you feel yourself being swayed from one side to another then back again, because it feels like you’re activating the deepest part of your humanity,” he continues. “It’s like a Russian nesting doll. You open one and there’s another inside… It’s one surprise after another,” added Shotgun Players Director Patrick Dooley. “A dominant theme that emerges in this story aligns with others that are addressed in the season, which is, what it means to be human.” Cast includes Erin Gould as Moderator/Jack Donovan, David Sinako as Dr. Alan James, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart as Dr. Sarah Matthis, Soren Santos as Professor Neel Serrano and Gabrielle Maalihan as Professor Lily Chan. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/show/the-motion/.

articles.text: The internationally acclaimed Bennewitz Quartet will perform at Kohl Mansion in Burlingame on October 19. Music at Kohl Mansion, the longest-running chamber-music-only presenter on the San Francisco peninsula, hosts the event. The program will feature quartet members Jakub Fiser and Stepan Jezek on violin, Jiri Pinkas on viola, and Stepan Dolezal on cello. Founded in 1998 and based in Prague, the Bennewitz Quartet has become one of the leading ensembles in international chamber music. The group received early recognition after winning top prizes at the Osaka Chamber Music and Festa (2005) and the Premio Paolo Borciani competition in Italy (2008). In 2019, the quartet was awarded the “Classic Prague Award” for Best Chamber Music Performance. Recent seasons have included performances at major European venues such as Wigmore Hall in London, Laeiszhalle in Hamburg, and Konzerthaus in Berlin. The ensemble has also appeared in the U.S., making its debut in cities including Providence, Houston, and Tucson, and returning to the Music and Beyond Festival in Ottawa and the Harvard Musical Association. In their home country, the Bennewitz Quartet recently completed a series of concerts featuring the complete string quartets of Antonín Dvořák as part of the Dvořák Prague Festival. A pre-concert talk by Stanford cellist and educator Christopher Costanza is held at 6 p.m., and the concert begins at 7 p.m. A complimentary wine and dessert reception follows the concert at 9 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, contact the Box Office at (650) 762-1130, or purchase online at https://musicatkohl.org/. articles.text: Piedmont artists and Art Walk veterans Irene Nelson, Chris Harvey, and Larraine Seiden will participate in the 51st annual ArtSpan San Francisco Open Studios later this month. The three will exhibit together as guest artists at Miro Studios, 744 Alabama St., San Francisco, on Sept. 27–28, 11 a.m.–5 p.m. The monthlong event, running Sept. 20–Oct. 19, invites the public to explore hundreds of artists’ studios across San Francisco neighborhoods. Visitors can connect directly with creators, discover new work, and experience the city through its thriving art community. Admission is free. A full guide is available at artspan.org. Artist Spotlights Irene Nelson creates abstract paintings as acts of discovery, blending memory, imagination, and experimentation. Her work has been shown at the de Young Museum, the Contemporary Jewish Museum, and the Crocker Art Museum, and is held in public and private collections worldwide. articles.text: A River Runs Through It, released in 1992, is a gently told period drama, beautifully photographed by Oscar-winning Philipe. Rousselot. It is set in Missoula, Montana, during a time that stretches from the end of WWI to the beginning of the Great Depression. The narrative, with voiceover by director Robert Redford, is based on the 1976 autobiography by Norman Maclean. The film follows the Maclean brothers, Norman (Craig Scheffer) and Paul (Brad Pitt), who as youngsters thrived in the bucolic surrounds of rural Missoula. They were taught the discipline, if not the art, of fly fishing on the nearby Blackfoot River by their Presbyterian minister father (Tom Skerritt) who gently merged religion with the early mornings the three spent standing in the rippling river, casting their lines out onto the eddying, rippling surface. Their time together, often spent sitting among the Ponderosa pines on the river’s banks, or finding a metronomic rhythm as they fished, moments when the morning light shimmered off the wet rocks, all of it a metaphor for their union, captured in the lyrical words of Maclean and spoken Tom Skerritt, Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt in A River Runs Through It

articles.text: John Greenleaf Whittier observed: “for all sad words of tongue or pen, the saddest are these: “it might have been.” Sounds like a hymn to regret. But not if you learn an important lesson from Dr. Ephraim Engleman. To him, life was a football field with an open field ahead of him. Prepare to be amazed and inspired. Born in San Jose in 1911, he was a musical child prodigy on the violin and the piano. He found early success playing music in silent film houses to accompany the silent films. Then the sound films made the scene, ending his nascent musical career. His parents suggested a medical career. That sounded good. But this child genius found it tough going. He made it through Stanford Medical School, but it was not as easy as playing music. Success and fame did come. Music and medicine have had a long connection. Consider the many doctors’ orchestras in our country. Dr. Engleman became a famous rheumatologist. His office at the University of California Medical Center overlooked San Francisco‘s Kezar Stadium. This was just the place to entertain contributors to his Rosalind Russell-Ephraim Engleman Research Center. The symbiosis of medicine and music continued until his 104th year. He died at his work desk. His enthusiasm for life was unbated. He believed that life was to be enjoyed and music was one of the most important aspects. He played his violin every day. Along the way, he met many famous musicians. Early on, he played string quartets with the illustrious violinist Misha Elman. He also acquired a collection of famous violins. Whether it was a Stradivarius or a Guarnerious, Eph had one. He also had a childlike enthusiasm which some mistook for boasting. For example, just about every famous violinist who came to San Francisco telephoned Eph and asked to come to visit him. Naturally, they tried the famous violins om jis collection, and a free concert ensued. The names of these musicians comprise a veritable Who’s Who of the music world. Somehow, this busy doctor found time to write an autobiography, many musical plays, and also compose popular songs. He also found time to play jazz piano and of course the regular chamber music sessions. Towards the end of his 104 years, Engleman offered some “commandments” for a good life. If I remember correctly, the first commandment was: “Choose your parents wisely.” Another was: “Never retire.” And be sure to enjoy everything that you do. Dr. Ephraim Engleman

articles.text: A scene from Happy Feet Happy Feet is charming and playful, making this rollicking tale of a unique penguin named Mumble (Elijah Wood) seem decidedly fresh. Apparently, every Emperor penguin sings a unique song called a “heartsong,” used to attract a mate. If the males’ song matches the females’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. Mumble soon becomes a young adult whose feet never stop moving; however it’s the elders, led by Noah (Hugo Weaving), who grumpily take exception to Mumble’s dancing and ridicules him, in his Scottish brogue, for being different. Meanwhile, he does have a secret crush on the talented Gloria (Brittany Murphy), but doesn’t have the “heartsong” that is so necessary to find a companion. Meanwhile, Mumble meets a group of mini-Mexican Adelie penguins, called “the Amigos,” whose leader is Ramon Lovelace (Robin Williams) who is willing to help Mumble court Gloria (Ramon sings “My Way” while Mumble lip-synchs). Naturally, Gloria falls for him. Soon all the young penguins are singing and tap dancing to “Boogie Wonderland.” Of course the elders are appalled. Mumble is ordered to stop, but refuses, and is exiled from the flock, blamed for what has been a lean fishing season. And so Mumble’s the adventure begins, one that takes him all the way to Australia where he ends up in a marine sanctuary where kids, one girl in particular, can stand and watch him swimming behind massive panes of glass pool. The girl taps on the glass and Mumble, with his beak, taps back, hoping to communicate with the humans. Event ually, Mumble is released from the sanctuary and finds his way home to his flock. It’s upon his return that he challenges the elders and prevails, and soon everyone is dancing and celebrating, most especially Mumble and Gloria and Ramon. Happy Feet. Directed by George Miller. With voices of Elijah Wood, Robin Williams, Brittany Murphy. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2008. Streaming on Prime/Apple tv/Fandango/ YouTube

articles.text: by Robert Redford. “In the slanting sun of the late afternoon the shadows of great branches reached from across the river, and the trees took the river in their arms. The shadows continued up the bank until they included us.” Regrettably, Norman Maclean passed away before the film was completed; however, his words frame a final, touching moment as Maclean, now nearing the end of his life, stands at the edge of the river, and with trembling hands slowly ties a fly to his line, and seemingly lost in the moment gazes off into the distance. “Eventually, all things merge into one, and the river runs through it. The river was cut by the world’s great flood and runs over rocks from the basement of time. On some of the rocks are timeless raindrops. Under the rocks are the words, and some of the words are theirs. I am haunted by waters.” It was only later that I learned that Robert Redford, at the age of 89, had died. And though I knew that decades had passed since I sat in a theater and watched Barefoot in the Park (1967), a romantic comedy with Jane Fonda, I took his timeless presence on the screen for granted. I gave little thought to the span of his career that began with an unaccredited role in 1960 and did not conclude until 2018 with his last leading role in the film The Old Man and the Gun. Yet he seemed to defy the gravity of aging. He would always be the Hubbell Gardiner in the film The Way We Were. His filmography is stunning,

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, September 24, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday From Havens’ estate to SB 9 homes: walkers trace Piedmont’s past and future By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was what locals call a hot day in Piedmont with temperatures in the 80s. The Walking on Wednesdays group stayed in the central part of town to avoid steep climbs. Even in the heat, 42 walkers and two K-9 best friends turned out at the Exedra for the weekly outing. A month earlier on August 6 the group had toured shaded Wildwood Gardens, once part of Frank C. Havens’ early-20th-century Wildwood Estate. That day they covered the two lower loops but ran out of time before reaching the upper section. Last week’s walk was a chance to complete it. Before setting out, walkers heard a quick refresher on Havens. Born in 1848 into a founding family of Shelter Island, New York, he left home at 16 to work as a cabin boy and sailed around Cape Horn to California. He spent time in Honolulu and China before arriving in San Francisco in 1866. Havens worked in banking, became an Oakland attorney, and emerged as a leading East Bay real estate developer, leaving a mark on Oakland, Berkeley and Piedmont. Construction is never far away in Piedmont, and the walkers saw plenty of it. They first detoured down Magnolia Avenue to the city’s new aquatics center. Earlier this month, both pools were filled and system testing began. Through the fencing, walkers could glimpse the sparkling pools, landscaping, and workers putting on final touches. Four water-blue letters spelling SWIM stood ready to welcome future visitors. The group followed a scenic path through upper Piedmont Park, past the Tea House and along Highland and Wildwood avenues to the old Wildwood Gardens entrance, still marked by two partially hidden stone columns. Skipping the lower loops from their August walk, they continued uphill. One stop was at a lot where foundation work for a new accessory dwelling unit had just begun. A deep pit carved into the hillside caught their attention. A worker, Octavio, explained that roughly 1,500 cubic yards of soil were being removed and that temporary piers and retaining walls kept the slope stable. He expected foundation work to wrap up by year’s end, with the house completed by late 2026. The walkers then continued past a backyard treehouse to the seldom-visited Wistaria Way loop. A nearby parcel had once been part of a larger home. After the owner died earlier this decade, the lot was donated to a church and sold in 2022. Two proposals that year for a single-family house were denied after objections from neighbors and the city about size. The owners then turned to Senate Bill 9, California’s 2022 law that lets homeowners split lots and build up to four units on parcels zoned for single-family homes. Their application, to divide the lot and build two homes plus an ADU, was approved by Piedmont planners in December 2023. Building permits followed in July 2024, and work started immediately. Today, the modern, glass-fronted structures are largely framed. Some finishing remains, but they already stand out. On a Wistaria walk last fall, owner Geoff Gibson told the group he hoped to spend Christmas 2025 there with his family. From the looks of progress, that may happen. The walk wrapped up by climbing Woodland Way to Lafayette Avenue, then back to the Exedra via Crocker, Wildwood, Sheridan and Highland avenues. It was a warm morning, with equal measures of local history, construction updates and neighborhood views. Coach P: The two seasons as well as offseasons do not overlap, so while it has been a challenge balancing my personal life along with the two sports, the sports themselves have not been too tough to balance. Q: What’s the most unforgettable game or meet you’ve coached so far? Coach P: The 2024 game against Newark is a game I will remember for a long time. That was the most prep I put into any game thus far, and our athletes came out and had our best week of practice all season. It was our last game of what was a historic season, so we wanted to make sure we came out ready to end the season on a positive note and also set the tone for varsity, who was also looking to secure their backto-back league title. I remember tons of nuances about the game, but a play that still gives me goosebumps is when we were up 13-7 late in the 4th quarter with Newark driving. They were on our 22-yard line, 2nd and 2, in position to score. But then here comes Max [Fujimoto], jumping an out route, picking it off, and going 80 yards for the pick six go-ahead touchdown. Game, set, match, and we ended the season on a five-game winning streak. Q: What were some challenges you faced in your first year, and how did you overcome them? A very sleek 2007 red Lotus Elise and to get people to know that we are here for them.” This was the first PPD car show with Frederick Shavies as Piedmont Police Chief, allowing residents an opportunity to meet him and other local first responders. “I think what Officer Petit has built on and has grown - over 100 classic and exotic cars – is incredible,” said Chief Shavies. “I’m happy to see so many members of our community, from infants to seniors, out enjoying themselves and enjoying the cars. And I’m happy that folks that have put so much labor and love into these vehicles are able to show them off. It’s incredible.” Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, Coast Construction Company brought a track car system for kids and parents to race their favorite cars in miniature. Residents also enjoyed food from a taco truck and conversations among the many car enthusiasts. “This is the result of hundreds of hours from five knuckleheads,” laughed resident Peter Gaylord about his car – a charmingly eclectic Dodge Colt plastered with stickers, racing colors, and several brass instrument horns. Gaylord, along with fellow resident Luis Zuniga, were at the event representing a group of friends who built the car to race in the 24 Hours of Lemons – a racing event for cars under $500. Officers came to support the car show from the Alameda County Sheriff’s Department, including the Alameda County Sheriff Yesenia Sanchez and District Attorney Ursula Jones Dickson. Residents and police officers enjoy the wide array of classic and custom vehicles at the 4th annual Coffee, Cars and Cops car show in Piedmont on Saturday, September 20. A racetrack for miniature cars was brought to the event by Coast Construction Company. Piedmonters and visitors wander through an array of nearly 150 vehicles at Piedmont’s 4th Annual Car Show. This family elected to enjoy the car show from the bed of an army truck.
